headline: Southwest Ledge Turns Cold and Green — Big Bass Holding, Bonito Showing Early on the East Side
subhead: The water broke clean off the Ledge this week, and the bass that showed up with it are the kind you tell stories about all winter.
body_markdown:
I felt it before I saw it. Ran out to the Ledge Tuesday morning and the water had that particular green-black color it gets when the cold pushes up from the bottom and meets the warm surface layer — like somebody drew a line across the ocean. That's the upwelling doing its thing off the Southwest Ledge, and when that line shows up in July, you stop what you're doing and go fish it.

The bass have been on that break all week. Not everywhere — you have to find the exact seam where the green water meets the blue — but where it's right, it's been the best stretch of big-fish action I've had since June. We're talking 30 to 40-pound class stripers, the real deal, holding in 40 to 60 feet of water on the west and southwest edges of the Ledge, working the last two hours of the ebb into the start of the flood. That current edge stacks bait against the structure and the big cows sit underneath it, not chasing, just waiting.

I've been running live eels on a three-way rig with just enough weight to hold bottom in that current — 6 to 8 ounces depending on how hard it's ripping — and I'm getting bit within the first twenty minutes most mornings. Umbrella rigs pulled slow through the same water have worked too, but the eels have out-produced everything else three to one this week. If you're bucktailing, go heavy — 2 to 3 ounces with a white or chartreuse tail — and let it sink all the way to the bottom before you start that slow lift-and-drop. The fish are hugging structure, not chasing anything up high.

The North Rip has been more of a mixed bag. I had one morning out there where we boated four fish over 25 pounds in an hour on the last of the outgoing, then it just shut off like someone flipped a switch when the tide went slack. That's the North Rip in July — it's a tide-dependent bite, and if you're not there for that window, you're just burning gas. I'd plan around the two hours either side of max ebb and don't waste your time on the slack.

Fluke have been the more reliable meal ticket if you want steady action instead of trophy hunting. Inside the Great Salt Pond and out along the sandy stretches toward Cow Cove, we've been picking through a lot of shorts to find keepers in the 18 to 22-inch range, mostly on white Gulp Swimming Mullets tipped with squid strips, fished on 3/4-ounce bucktails drifted slow over clean bottom in 15 to 25 feet. The morning bite has been better than the afternoon — once the sun gets high and the boat traffic picks up in the Pond, the bite gets nervous.

Bluefish have shown up in good numbers off the East Side, and I mean good-sized blues, not the snappers you get in the harbor. Working birds have been easy to spot from a half mile out — diving terns over busting fish, usually just outside the surf line off Mohegan Bluffs. Poppers and small metal, Deadly Dicks and Kastmasters in the half-ounce to one-ounce range, have been getting hit as soon as they land. Watch your fingers with these — this year's class has real teeth on them.

And here's the one that's got guys at the dock talking: bonito showed up early this week off the southeast corner, working bait pods in close to the rips. It's early for them — usually we don't see bonito in numbers until late July or August — but the water's been warm enough and the bait's been thick enough that a few showed up ahead of schedule. Small profile epoxy jigs and Albie Snax in the smaller sizes have worked when you can get in front of them. It's not a full-blown run yet, just a preview, but it's worth keeping a rod rigged for it if you're already out there for bass.

Worth noting — squid have been showing up in good concentrations around the island and up toward Narragansett Bay this week, and that's typically the signal that things are about to get busier out here. Bait like that pulling into the area usually means the bass numbers build through late July rather than thin out, especially with water temps holding steady in the low-to-mid 60s out at depth and warmer up top.

Looking ahead, the tides are building toward the new moon, which should mean stronger current through the Ledge and the rips for the next several days — that's usually good news for the eel bite, since these fish want that moving water. If the wind stays out of the southwest and doesn't blow the structure to pieces, I'd put my time on the Southwest Ledge in that morning ebb window and keep a fluke rod rigged for when the tide slacks off. The North Rip is worth a look but only if you can be there right at that tide change — otherwise you're fishing empty water.
